issues.title: amneziawg-installer: One-command AmneziaWG setup for Ubuntu/Debian VPS (3.1 by default since v6.0.0)
issues.body:
[[AmneziaWG](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amneziawg-go)](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amneziawg-go) has been discussed here before (#223, #88), but deploying it on a VPS still requires significant manual effort: building the kernel module, configuring obfuscation parameters, setting up firewall rules, and managing clients.

[**[amneziawg-installer](https://github.com/bivlked/amneziawg-installer)**](https://github.com/bivlked/amneziawg-installer) is a Bash toolkit that automates the full AmneziaWG 2.0 deployment on a dedicated Ubuntu (24.04 LTS / 25.10 / 26.04) or Debian (12 / 13) server in a single command. It targets users who want a working VPN on a clean minimal VPS without advanced Linux knowledge.

**What it does:**

- Installs AmneziaWG 2.0 with full protocol support (H1-H4 ranges, S1-S4 padding, I1-I5 CPS concealment packets, Jc/Jmin/Jmax junk packets); all obfuscation parameters are generated automatically
- Hardens the server: UFW deny-all + SSH rate-limit + VPN port only, Fail2Ban, sysctl hardening, IPv6 disabled by default (configurable via `--allow-ipv6`)
- Optimizes kernel and network stack based on detected hardware (RAM, CPU, NIC capabilities)
- Provides client management: add, remove, list, regenerate, backup/restore; outputs both `.conf` files and QR codes
- Survives reboots mid-install via a state machine that resumes from the last completed step
- Non-interactive mode with CLI flags for scripted deployments

**AmneziaWG 2.0 vs 1.x:**

The installer uses AmneziaWG 2.0, which adds CPS (Concealment Packet System) with tagged I1-I5 parameters and range-based H1-H4 headers, making traffic patterns significantly harder to fingerprint compared to AWG 1.x fixed values.

**Relevance to censorship circumvention:**

AmneziaWG modifies the WireGuard protocol at the packet level: randomized headers, junk packets, and variable padding make it resistant to the DPI signatures that censors use to block standard WireGuard (as reported in Russia #274, Iran #140, Turkmenistan #523). A user in Turkmenistan (#523) reported AmneziaWG surviving on the same IP for ~2 years, though with very low traffic (~500 MB/month); similar setups with higher consumption were banned. This installer removes the deployment barrier by handling the entire setup automatically.

issues.title: Title: Feature request: Allow disabling automatic TUN prefix routes on Linux
issues.body:
**Problem**

On Linux, Yggdrasil automatically creates a connected route for the TUN interface's IPv6 prefix. For example:

```200::/7 dev ygg0 proto kernel metric 256 pref medium```

I run multiple Yggdrasil-go instances (v0.5.15) using Docker with network_mode: host. Each instance has a different GroupPassword, and I want to route traffic to specific Yggdrasil subnet prefixes (e.g. 300:...::/64) through the corresponding TUN interface.

Because all instances share the host's network namespace and routing table, I would like to manage these routes explicitly instead of relying on the automatically created 200::/7 route.

**Proposed solution**

Could you add an optional configuration parameter, for example:

```IfNoPrefixRoute: true```

On Linux, when enabled, Yggdrasil would set the IFA_F_NOPREFIXROUTE flag when assigning the TUN IPv6 address. This would prevent the kernel from automatically creating the connected route for that address prefix.

The default value should remain false to preserve existing behavior.

**Expected behavior**

The TUN interface and its IPv6 address are created normally.

With IfNoPrefixRoute: true, the kernel does not automatically install the connected route for the TUN address prefix.

Administrators can add explicit routes to selected Yggdrasil subnets through the appropriate TUN interfaces.

Existing behavior remains unchanged when the option is not enabled.

**Use case**

Running multiple Yggdrasil instances with different GroupPassword values in Docker using host networking, while routing selected 300:...::/64 subnet prefixes through specific instances.

I can manage the routes manually using Linux ip -6 route commands. The goal is to make this setup possible without maintaining a custom Yggdrasil build.

Would this feature be appropriate for upstream?

issues.title: fix Makefile.linux logic, improve readability
Check read and write results for torrent files and reopen a broken stream
issues.body:
As asked in #dev by orignal and R4SAS.

`TorrentFile::Save` and `Load` did not look at the result of the write or the read, so a failed write was reported as success. Worse, the failure leaves the error flag set on the stream while the file stays open, and `Open` only opens when the file is closed - so every later call failed silently for the life of the object, while `m_LastAccessTime` kept being updated so the file was not closed by inactivity either.

Now both calls check the stream after the operation, log the error with `strerror` and return false, and `Open` closes and clears a stream that is open but in a failed state before reopening it. The periodic flush is checked too, since that is where a buffered write actually reaches the disk.

Measured with a harness that sets `RLIMIT_FSIZE` to 64 KB and writes past it:

| step | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| write at offset 0 | true | true |
| write past the size limit | true | true (buffered, see below) |
| write at offset 2048 after the failure | true (nothing written) | false |
| read at offset 0 | false | true |

The file on disk holds 1024 bytes in both cases - that is, the second and third writes were lost while reporting success. After the change the lost write is reported, and the stream recovers for the next call instead of staying broken.

One honest limitation: writes are buffered, so a write that oversteps a limit still returns true at that moment and the error surfaces on the next call or on the flush. Forcing a flush per block would make it immediate, but that is a different trade-off on disk IO, so I left it to you. Build without warnings, unit tests pass.

issues.title: Request an expired encrypted LeaseSet by its blinded key
issues.body:
**What this does not do:** it does not keep the expired LeaseSet. That is erased exactly as before,
in the same place, on the same condition.

**What it keeps:** the unblinded public key of the remote destination, 32 bytes plus two signature
types, in a map next to the LeaseSet cache. Blinding depends on the date and is computed at lookup
time from the current date, so the stored value does not go stale at the day boundary. An entry is
dropped 600 seconds after it was last used, so a destination that went away for good does not stay
in memory.

**Why it is needed at all.** A destination published as encrypted is stored under its blinded hash.
`RequestDestination` receives only the ident hash, and the blinded key is derived from the full
identity, which lived in the LeaseSet and is gone once the LeaseSet is erased. An ident hash is a
hash, so nothing can be derived back from it: without the key kept somewhere, the request cannot be
formed at all. This is not "the cached LeaseSet is stale", it is "there is no way to ask".

Streaming already does this: a stream keeps the remote identity for its lifetime and re-requests by
the blinded key when the LeaseSet expires. A datagram session keeps only the ident hash and is
dropped after ten minutes of silence, so nothing survives to ask with. This change gives datagram
sessions the same ability, at the destination level rather than per session.

**What it looks like without the change.** An incoming datagram carries the sender identity, so the
link recovers only if the encrypted destination speaks first. If our side speaks first, it never
reaches the peer. In practice an encrypted destination stops working as a server for datagram
applications after any pause.

**Measured** on two routers in the live network with SAM datagram sessions on both sides. One
destination has `i2cp.leaseSetType=5`, a plain one next to it on the same router is the control.
The peers exchange datagrams, stay idle for 13 minutes, then the other side sends first, 5 attempts
each:

- before: nothing arrives at the encrypted destination in two runs, its ident hash "was not found
  on 7 floodfills" in the log; the control receives on attempt 3 and 2
- after: the encrypted destination receives on attempt 4 and 3, the control on attempt 3 and 2

Re-checked later on the head of the day: encrypted reached on attempt 2, control on attempt 2.

Builds with no new warnings, `make -C tests` passes.

issues.title: XHTTP server: Raise HTTP/2 receive windows for faster uplink
issues.body:
## Summary

The XHTTP h1/h2 server uses `net/http`'s HTTP/2 defaults: 1 MiB receive window per connection and per stream. All uplink traffic on one h2 connection (stream-up, stream-one, and packet-up over XMUX) shares that window, so uplink is capped at ~1 MiB per RTT, about 160 Mbit/s at 50 ms RTT and lower on longer paths.

This sets `http.Server.HTTP2` to 64 MiB per connection and 16 MiB per stream, in line with the `x/net/http2` client transport defaults (1 GiB / 4 MiB). Buffers are only allocated as data arrives. It's server-only, so existing clients benefit without changes. XHTTP/3 (QUIC windows) is not affected.

## Test

VLESS + XHTTP + REALITY, stock 26.10.21 client (macOS) → Linux server, 52 ms RTT, iperf3 12 s through the tunnel (Mbit/s):

| mode | up ×1 | up ×8 | down ×1 | down ×8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| stream-one, before | 76 | 171 | 156 | 367 |
| stream-one, after | 271 | 503 | 191 | 388 |
| packet-up, before | 140 | 341 | 169 | 421 |
| packet-up, after | 253 | 459 | 153 | 433 |

Download differences are within run-to-run noise; uplink improves 1.3–3.6×.

issues.title: Inbound: Close and remove the handler when it fails to start
issues.body:
`inbound.Manager.AddHandler` first puts the handler into `taggedHandlers` (or `untaggedHandlers`) and, when the manager is already running, then calls `handler.Start()` and returns its error. Nothing is undone when `Start` fails.

This is the path of `HandlerService.AddInbound` (`xray api adi`). If the new inbound cannot start, for example because one of its ports is already in use, the API returns the error but the handler stays in the manager. Adding it again with the same tag fails with `existing tag found` until it is removed by hand, and the workers that did start (the ports before the busy one in a port range) keep listening.

Now a handler that fails to start is taken out of the manager again and closed, so the ports it opened are released and the tag can be used again. Startup is not affected: handlers from the config are only started later by `Manager.Start`.

Verified with the new `TestAddHandlerFailedStart`, which adds a tagged and an untagged handler whose `Start` fails to a running manager, and then adds the tag again. On main it fails with:

    handler "in" was not closed after failing to start
    handler "in" is still registered after failing to start (1 handlers)

With this change it passes. I also checked it end to end with a dokodemo-door inbound on two ports where the second one was busy: on main the first port stayed bound after the failed add, and adding the inbound again after freeing the port failed with `existing tag found: in`. With the change the first port is free again and the second add works.

Also ran `go test ./app/proxyman/inbound/...` (also with `-race`), `go test ./testing/scenarios -run TestCommander`, `go vet ./app/proxyman/inbound/...`, gofmt and `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./`.

It bundles REALITY `83f6217`, which is the current REALITY `main`. v26.7.28 (REALITY `9234c77`) has the same code, and that's where I first noticed it. The `ServerName: sni` probe config involved has been in place since the per-SNI detection was added in REALITY `21af070` (June 2025).

### Summary

REALITY copies the target's post-handshake records (NewSessionTicket) for every name in `serverNames` except the empty one, `""`. For `""`, the startup probe `DetectPostHandshakeRecordsLens` fails before it sends anything, and the failure is silent. The key for empty SNI then gets `[]int{}`, so authenticated clients without SNI get no post-handshake records at all, even when the target sends them to a client without SNI.

This is the same mismatch [Aparecium](https://github.com/ban6cat6/aparecium) exploits (#4778), the one the post-handshake record imitation was added to fix. For connections without SNI, that fix has no effect, and Aparecium still detects them.

### Why this matters

No-SNI is a documented REALITY feature: see `serverName` in the [REALITY docs](https://xtls.github.io/en/config/transports/reality.html), which say "the server-side `serverNames` must contain an empty string `""`". It is also useful in practice right now. In Russia, connecting without SNI is one of the ways around the newer SNI-based restrictions, sometimes working better than ClientHello fragmentation, and it is easier to set up in many clients than fragmentation is. So it shouldn't be dismissed as a niche option. Users who turn it on fingerprint themselves without knowing it: they get weaker camouflage than the other names on the same inbound, with no warning. The fix is two lines, only touches the startup probe, and doesn't change behaviour for named entries.

### Cause

[`record_detect.go#L61`](https://github.com/XTLS/REALITY/blob/83f621788ca88b83179810b12baa7ae518aacb83/record_detect.go#L61) and [`#L96`](https://github.com/XTLS/REALITY/blob/83f621788ca88b83179810b12baa7ae518aacb83/record_detect.go#L96) both build the probe's config like this:

```go
uConn := utls.UClient(detectConn, &utls.Config{
	ServerName: sni, // "" for the empty entry
	NextProtos: nextProtos,
}, fingerprint)
```

uTLS refuses a ClientHello that has an empty `ServerName` while certificate verification is on ([`handshake_client.go#L53`](https://github.com/refraction-networking/utls/blob/aa6edf4b11af82e110eea845bb2983d30138d651/handshake_client.go#L53)):

```
tls: at least one of ServerName, InsecureSkipVerify or InsecureServerNameToVerify must be specified in the tls.Config
```

So `Handshake()` returns before anything is sent, and the deferred function ([`record_detect.go#L32`](https://github.com/XTLS/REALITY/blob/83f621788ca88b83179810b12baa7ae518aacb83/record_detect.go#L32)) stores `[]int{}` for `"<target>  0"`, `"<target>  1"` and `"<target>  2"`. Later, [`tls.go#L411-L419`](https://github.com/XTLS/REALITY/blob/83f621788ca88b83179810b12baa7ae518aacb83/tls.go#L411-L419) looks up that key for every authenticated connection without SNI and writes nothing. The second probe, the ChangeCipherSpec one at `#L96`, fails the same way, so `GlobalMaxCSSMsgCount` is never set for these keys either.

To check the stored values directly, I called `reality.DetectPostHandshakeRecordsLens` from a small program and dumped `GlobalPostHandshakeRecordsLens` 15 s later.

issues.title: Direct/Freedom outbound: Fix `blockDelay` for DispatchLink() inbounds such as VLESS, Hysteria, etc.
issues.body:
Regression from #6060 (958eb9e). `blackhole` waits for `buf.Copy(input, buf.Discard)` and relies on the `blockDelay` timer calling `common.Interrupt(input)` to end it. That only works for a pipe: VLESS, Hysteria and other inbounds that use `DispatchLink` pass a reader on the client connection, and `Interrupt` does nothing to it. So a blocked connection stays open until the client closes it, whatever `blockDelay` is. In our tests it was still open after 330 s, longer than `connIdle`.

Drain the input in a goroutine and return once the delay has passed or the input has ended. The inbound then closes the connection, as it does after the blackhole outbound.

`TestVlessBlockDelay` covers `blockDelay` 0 and 1 through a VLESS inbound. Both cases fail on main.

issues.title: Preserve buffered bytes before returning read errors
issues.body:
`BufferedReader.Read` discards a nonempty `MultiBuffer` whenever the underlying reader returns an error with its data. This is a valid `io.Reader` result: a local TLS 1.2 reproduction delivers an application record and `close_notify` together, and `crypto/tls.Conn` returns `4, "ping", io.EOF`. `SingleReader` preserves those bytes, but the buffered adapter returns `0, io.EOF`.

Keep the error until the buffered bytes have been consumed, including when callers switch between `Read`, `ReadAtMost`, `ReadMultiBuffer` and `WriteTo`. The cached writer flush retains its existing handling; a pending read error is returned before another underlying read.

Five regression cases cover data with EOF, mixed read methods, partial reads followed by `WriteTo`, and a non-EOF error that must be reported once without an extra read. The cases fail on the original implementation and pass after the fix.

Validation:
- Deterministic local TLS reproduction and separate-record controls pass with the fix; certificate verification remains enabled.

issues.title: sockopt.interface: when the interface does not exist, the dial silently goes unbound (can loop back into TUN)
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

If an outbound has `streamSettings.sockopt.interface` set and that interface does not exist at dial time, Xray does not fail the dial. It logs `failed to apply socket options > failed to get interface ...` at **Info** level and opens the connection without any binding, so it follows the system routing table.

`transport/internet/system_dialer.go` (v26.10.10, lines 134-139; same in v26.9.9) only logs the error returned by `applyOutboundSocketOptions` and goes on to `dialer.DialContext`. The UDP path does the same (lines 77-81). The error itself comes from `net.InterfaceByName` in `transport/internet/sockopt_darwin.go:136-140`. From reading the source, Linux takes the same path (the error is logged, not returned); I tested macOS only.

Why this matters. A typical full-tunnel setup on a desktop routes everything into a TUN interface handled by Xray (default route split as 0.0.0.0/1 + 128.0.0.0/1 into the TUN), and binds outbounds with `sockopt.interface` so that their own sockets do not enter the TUN again. If the bound interface goes away, the fallback sends the outbound's sockets into the TUN, Xray routes them to the same outbound, and the connection loops.

We hit this loop in practice on macOS. A separate OpenVPN client provided a corporate network through its own utun interface, and the corporate subnet was routed to a freedom outbound so that it would follow that VPN's route. At night the OpenVPN client lost its connection and its utun interface was removed. From then on, every connection to the corporate subnet (including DNS queries to the corporate DNS server) entered the TUN, came back to the same outbound and entered the TUN again. When we looked, there were about 8,000 looped connections, all 16,384 ephemeral ports were in use, and other processes on the host got `EADDRNOTAVAIL` (`Can't assign requested address`) on connect until the loop was broken by restarting Xray.

In that incident the outbound had no `sockopt.interface` at all, so the loop itself is a config problem. The obvious fix is to bind the outbound to the other VPN's interface (`"interface": "utunN"`), so that it can never fall into the TUN. That does not work because of this issue: once the interface disappears, the binding is skipped and the loop is back. The only visible sign is an Info-level log line, which is hidden at the usual `warning` level.

Expected: if the interface named in `sockopt.interface` cannot be found, the dial fails (fail closed), as a bound socket does when its interface has no route. At the very least the error should be logged as a warning. A silent fallback to the routing table defeats the purpose of binding: it can send traffic into a tunnel (loop) or past it (leak).

### Reproduction Method

No server and no TUN are needed. Run Xray with the config below (interface `utun99` does not exist) and send a request through the SOCKS inbound:

```
curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://example.com/
```

Result: HTTP 200. The log shows that the interface was not found and the connection was opened anyway; its local endpoint is the address of whatever interface the routing table chose (on our machine, the address of a TUN interface that held the default route).

For comparison, with `"interface": "en0"` the same request goes out through en0 (local endpoint is en0's address) and no error is logged.

Expected result: the connection through the outbound bound

issues.title: Sockopt: Handle single-family interface binding on Windows, including TUN inbound's `autoOutboundsInterface`
issues.body:
With `autoOutboundsInterface` selecting an IPv4-only Windows adapter, a normal IPv4 UDP dial can fail with WSAEINVAL (10022). Go creates a dual-stack socket and reports `udp6`; TUN then requires both IPv6 and IPv4 interface bindings, although IPv6 is disabled on the selected adapter. IPv6-only interfaces have the corresponding IPv4-binding failure. IPv6 TCP is also unnecessarily subjected to IPv4 binding.

Keep both bindings for dual-stack UDP. If binding fails, use the existing `BindError` classification to permit one Windows UDP socket-creation retry restricted to the resolved destination's family. The TUN helper checks `IPV6_V6ONLY` and applies IPv4 options only when the UDP socket supports both families; IPv6 TCP/IP binds only IPv6.

**Why retain dual-stack first?** Freedom's packet writer can send different destinations through one UDP socket. Binding only the initial destination's family could leave the other family unbound. This change preserves mixed-family UDP when both bindings work. A single-family retry cannot emit packets on the unsupported family, and a failure to bind the required family remains fatal. Ordinary external-controller errors are not retried. No configuration fields or public APIs change.

Related to #7160 and the [follow-up discussion on #7201](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7201#issuecomment-6314278104); this does not claim to explain every occurrence of the original error.

### Validation

Native Windows 10/amd64 in Hyper-V, Go 1.27.2, comparing unmodified `00c0277787c84425738b5e65fe515b0473e06203` with this change. A disposable Wintun adapter was tested with both protocol bindings enabled, IPv6 disabled, and IPv4 disabled. Tests exercise the actual default dialer and TUN binding helper with local UDP/TCP echo traffic.

| Native scenario | Unmodified | Fixed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dual-stack UDP, including IPv4 and IPv6 destinations on one socket | Pass | Pass |
| IPv4-only uplink, IPv4 UDP with wildcard source | Fail | Pass |
| IPv6-only uplink, IPv6 UDP | Fail | Pass |
| IPv6-only uplink, IPv6 TCP | Fail | Pass |

IPv4-mapped destinations and explicit source addresses were also checked. Required-family failures remain fatal; restricted UDP sockets reject the opposite family without delivering its packet, and an ordinary controller denial produces exactly one attempt. Dual-stack interface bindings were read back from Winsock. The temporary adapter was removed; the existing guest core/ICS runtime, original adapters, forwarding settings and routes were preserved. This is native socket/traffic evidence, not a full TUN-ingress or throughput benchmark.

Affected package tests (`proxy/tun`, `transport/internet`, `proxy/socks`, `proxy/dns`), `go vet`, upstream `vformat`, and `git diff --check` passed. Transport tests cross-compiled for Linux/amd64 and macOS/arm64; they were not executed there. The full suite and race detector were not run locally. The native investigation fixture is kept outside the production diff.

issues.title: WebSocket: Treat normal close frames as io.EOF
issues.body:
## What this fixes

A WebSocket close frame with a normal status (1000) or no status (1005) ends the byte stream the same way a FIN does, but `connection.Read` surfaced gorilla's `*websocket.CloseError` to its callers.

VLESS and Trojan carry payload without framing, so a response copy ended with that error. `app/proxyman/outbound.Handler.Dispatch` treats every error other than `io.EOF` as a failure and calls `common.Interrupt`, which releases the data still buffered in the pipe before the inbound has read it. The client gets a short response that ends with a normal FIN - silent truncation for HTTP/1.0 responses without Content-Length, and a `websocket: close 1000 (normal)` line for every such connection.

Fix: map `websocket.IsCloseError(err, CloseNormalClosure, CloseNoStatusReceived)` to `io.EOF` in `connection.Read`. Other close codes keep their error semantics. The same wrapper is used by the XHTTP browser dialer client (`transport/internet/splithttp/browser_client.go`), so that path inherits the fix.

Fixes #7235.

## Test record

Environment: `1b1647cd` (v26.10.21), linux/amd64. The configs and scripts from the report used verbatim: target answers `HTTP/1.0 200 OK` + 65536 body bytes without Content-Length, then closes; the client fetches through an `http` inbound -> VLESS/ws outbound.

| scenario | base `1b1647cd` | with fix `bba46a28` |
|---|---|---|
| 20 sequential fetches, `GOMAXPROCS=1` | 19/20 short (15 x 0 B, 2 x 32749 B, 1 x 8171 B, 1 x 8173 B); 20 `close 1000` log lines | 20/20 complete 65536 B; 0 close lines |
| 10 rounds x 20 concurrent fetches | ~172/200 short; 200 `close 1000` log lines | 200/200 complete; 0 close lines |
| raw TCP control (same scripts) | 20/20 complete; 0 close lines | 20/20 complete |

The byte counts above are from the runs saved for this report; a second base run produced the same shape (18/20 short) with a different byte split.

Unit tests (new `connection_test.go`, real WebSocket server + the production wrapper): RED on base - close 1000 and 1005 come back as `websocket: close 1000 (normal)` / `close 1005 (no status)` instead of `io.EOF`; GREEN with the fix. A 1001 (`going away`) control asserts that other close codes stay errors, before and after.

`go test ./transport/internet/...` - 25 packages pass. `go build ./...`, `gofmt`, `go vet` clean.

Known boundary: a close frame arriving in the middle of a fragmented message still surfaces as a close error, because that payload is genuinely incomplete; only a close after a complete message is remapped, which is the reported mechanism.

issues.title: WireGuard kernelTun: Fix capget writing past its buffer
issues.body:
`KernelTunSupported` calls `capget` with `_LINUX_CAPABILITY_VERSION_3`. For v3 (and v2) the kernel always writes **two** `__user_cap_data_struct`, 24 bytes, one for capabilities 0-31 and one for 32-63 (see `capget(2)`). The code passes a single `unix.CapUserData`, 12 bytes, so the kernel writes 12 bytes past it, over whatever comes next on the goroutine stack.

On 64-bit this has gone unnoticed so far. On 32-bit ARM it overwrites a saved return address, and creating any WireGuard outbound kills the process. That includes `xray run -test` on a WireGuard config and every WireGuard config in Android clients on 32-bit-only phones. The panic message depends on the frame layout:

```
runtime: g 1: unexpected return pc for github.com/xtls/xray-core/common.CreateObject called from 0x18
fatal error: unknown caller pc
```
```
fatal error: traceback did not unwind completely
```
Sometimes it is a SIGSEGV inside `runtime.mallocgcSmallScanNoHeaderSC5`.

The bug came in with #3871 (2024-10-15).

### Reproduction
Samsung Galaxy A13 (SM-A135F), Android 14, 32-bit only (`armeabi-v7a`), `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm GOARM=7 CGO_ENABLED=0`, Go 1.27.3, v26.10.21 (`1b1647c`), any WireGuard outbound, `xray run -test -c wg.json`:

| build | result |
|---|---|
| default flags | crashes 3/3 |
| `-gcflags=all=-l=4` (release workflow flags) | passes, by luck of frame layout |
| `-gcflags=github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/wireguard=-N` | passes, by luck of frame layout |
| default flags + this fix | passes 3/3, VLESS config also passes |

The release binaries happen not to crash because `-l=4` moves things around. `gomobile bind` builds don't pass it, so v2rayNG 2.3.14 (AndroidLibXrayLite, Go 1.27.3, the same xray commit) crashes on every WireGuard delay test and connect on these phones. Other xray-based Android clients on the same phone also crash when starting WireGuard.

### Fix
Pass a `[2]unix.CapUserData` and read `data[0].Effective` (`CAP_NET_ADMIN` is 12, so it is in the first word). `go vet` is clean for linux/amd64, arm64, 386, arm and mips.

issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

### Description

Since v26.10.21 (REALITY `83f621788ca8`), every authenticated REALITY connection fails when the target sends an **empty EncryptedExtensions** (no SNI ack, no ALPN, nothing else). With `"show": true` the server prints:

```
hs.handshake() err: payload[0]: 8, padding: -4
```

v26.9.9 (REALITY `8cdf7bf9c7f0`) works with the same target.

Cause:

- XTLS/REALITY `3c98159` ("Sync upstream Go 1.27+", #30) added to `handshake_server_tls13.go`:
  ```go
  if !hs.c.didResume && hs.clientHello.serverName != "" {
      encryptedExtensions.serverNameAck = true
  }
  ```
  An authenticated connection always carries SNI unless `serverNames` contains `""`, so REALITY's own EncryptedExtensions now always has the 4-byte empty `server_name` extension. Before this commit `encryptedExtensionsMsg` had no such field.
- `[REALITY] SECTION: mimic recorded handshakeLen` in `conn.go` pads each handshake record to the length recorded from the target and returns `payload[0]: %v, padding: %v` when its own record is longer (`payload[0]: 8` is EncryptedExtensions).
- REALITY's own EncryptedExtensions has no ALPN, so it is now 4 bytes longer than an empty one. A target whose EncryptedExtensions is empty gives a 28-byte record (including the 5-byte record header) against REALITY's 32, hence padding -4. Any extension on the target side (an SNI ack, ALPN, ...) is at least 4 bytes and absorbs it.

Not setting `serverNameAck` in the REALITY server (the pre-sync behaviour) looks sufficient, since padding then matches any target; I have not tested a patch.

This is easy to miss: the fallback path does not reach this code, so probing the node without the key looks fine, and without `show` the server logs only an Info line (`REALITY: processed invalid connection ...: handshake did not complete successfully`) while the client gets EOF. We hit it on a production node whose target neither acks SNI nor negotiates ALPN. To check a target, look for any extension besides `supported versions` and `key share`:

```
openssl s_client -connect <Domain>:443 -servername <Domain> -tls1_3 -alpn h2,http/1.1 -tlsextdebug </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep 'TLS server extension'
```

All on loopback (Linux, OpenSSL 3.5.5). Three `openssl s_server` targets with the same self-signed certificate for `example.test`:

# A: empty EncryptedExtensions

# B: acks SNI (s_server acks only when -servername installs its callback and the name matches)
openssl s_server -accept 127.0.0.1:20444 -cert c.pem -key k.pem -tls1_3 -www -quiet -servername example.test -cert2 c.pem -key2 k.pem

issues.title: FakeDNS: add a shared mapping service and remote engine
issues.body:
Allow independent Xray processes on the same machine to use one authoritative FakeDNS allocator through the existing gRPC API.

## Why this is needed

A FakeDNS answer can be consumed by a different core from the one that generated it. For example, a Windows client may route host traffic through one TUN adapter/core and Internet Connection Sharing (ICS) traffic through a second TUN adapter/core, with different routing rules and outbounds. Both paths may receive synthetic addresses from the same DNS service.

If the DNS core returns `198.18.0.42` for `example.com`, the ICS traffic core must recover `example.com` when a shared client connects to that address. An independent FakeDNS instance either has no mapping or may have assigned the same address to a different domain. Using identical pool configuration does not synchronize those mappings. Forwarding DNS queries to the first core also does not give the traffic core access to its reverse map.

One shared allocator lets the separate cores recover the same domain and then apply their own routing policies, without duplicating FakeDNS allocation or coupling all traffic to one process. This is also useful for isolated traffic workers and replacing a traffic core while OS/application DNS caches still contain synthetic addresses. A single-core deployment, or a Go embedding already sharing one engine in-process, does not need this API.

## Implementation

Adds the opt-in `FakeDNSService` to commander:

| RPC | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `GetPools` | Discover initialized synthetic CIDRs. |
| `Allocate` | Allocate addresses using the authority's existing LRU, selecting IPv4 and/or IPv6. |
| `ReverseLookup` | Recover a domain from a synthetic address; an unknown or evicted address returns an empty domain. |

An explicit `fakedns.remote` engine implements the existing FakeDNS interfaces using one reusable gRPC connection. Pool membership is checked locally; allocations and reverse lookups consult the authority. There is no replicated reverse cache or fallback allocator that could disagree with the authority after eviction.

Optional context-aware mapping methods carry DNS/sniffing request cancellation, deadlines and backend errors across the RPC boundary. Existing local configurations and context-free engine interfaces remain supported. Startup validates pool discovery, failed startup closes its connection, and consumer shutdown cancels outstanding requests without closing the authority.

Example authority settings, alongside its normal DNS/inbound/routing configuration:

```json
{
  "api": {
    "tag": "api",
    "listen": "127.0.0.1:8080",
    "services": ["FakeDNSService"]
  },
  "fakedns": [
    { "ipPool": "198.18.0.0/15", "poolSize": 65535 },
    { "ipPool": "2001:2::/48", "poolSize": 65535 }
  ]
}
```

Each consumer selects that allocator instead of defining its own pools:

```json
{
  "fakedns": {
    "remote": { "address": "127.0.0.1:8080", "timeout": 2000 }
  }
}
```

Consumers retain the normal `fakedns` DNS server selection where needed and FakeDNS sniffing/destination override on their traffic inbounds. Local pool settings and `remote` are mutually exclusive. Configuration and lifecycle details are in `app/dns/fakedns/SHARING.md`.

## Access and scope

The new RPCs require a direct loopback TCP connection or a local Unix socket, checked against the accepted transport peer before accessing the engine. Routed API connections and forwarding metadata cannot establish local reach. Consumer endpoints accept loopback IP literals or absolute Unix socket paths and bypass proxy discovery.

This is a locality restriction, not local-user authentication; administrators must protect access to the API/socket. Existing RPC access behavior is unchanged.

The change adds no module dependencies, Windows/ICS implementation, real-DNS sharing, statistics API, or application-specific hooks. Protocol definitions and generated Go bindings are included.

## Lifecycle limits

Mappings survive consumer r

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable error responses
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `errorResponse` object to the XHTTP inbound settings, replacing the bare status-only rejections with a service-consistent appearance.

Currently every rejected request is answered with a bare status code: no body, no `Content-Type` (Go's default "404 page not found" or nothing at all). From the terminating side (CDN, reverse proxy, monitoring) a server that answers *every* unknown path with a naked status code and no content type does not look like a normal service.

- `body` and `contentType` apply to every error response the hub writes (404 unknown path, 400/405/409/413/500 etc.), giving all rejections a uniform, service-consistent appearance.
- `statusCode` overrides the status for requests failing the padding validation — the effective authentication gate — allowing 403 semantics instead of the default 400.
- When `errorResponse` is unset, the behavior is unchanged.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "errorResponse": {
    "statusCode": 403,
    "body": "{\"error\":\"forbidden\"}",
    "contentType": "application/json"
  }
}
```

Resulting surface: unknown paths → `404 {"error":"forbidden"}`, the API gate without valid padding → `403` with the same body — a coherent API host instead of a bare 404/400 machine.

## Notes

- Server-side only. Round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 (matches all existing `.pb.go` headers; unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain).
- Proto field `errorResponse = 31` — merges cleanly alongside #7247 (`responseHeaders = 30`); both features are independent.

## Tests

- `Test_WriteErrorResponse`: bare default when unset, configured body + content type, padding-reject status default (400) and override (403).
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable response headers
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `responseHeaders` map (`map<string, string>`) to the XHTTP inbound settings, giving the server control over the headers it writes on responses.

Currently the hub hardcodes a set of response headers: the CORS block for the browser dialer (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`), `X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control` and the SSE `Content-Type`. With `responseHeaders` an operator can add, override, or remove any of them, as well as set arbitrary extra response headers.

## Semantics

- A key that doesn't collide with a default header is added to every response.
- A key that matches a hardcoded header overrides it.
- An empty value removes that header from the response entirely (including the hardcoded ones).
- When `responseHeaders` is unset, the behavior is byte-identical to before.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "responseHeaders": {
    "Server": "nginx",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://example.com",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": ""
  }
}
```

## Why

- The CORS headers only matter for the browser dialer; a plain server deployment currently emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, which is undesirable behind a specific origin and gets flagged by security reviews.
- Reverse-proxy and CDN setups sometimes require specific response headers (`Server`, `Via`, custom headers) or different cache semantics.
- Operators running behind intermediaries may want the response header set to stay consistent with the profile of the service they front, instead of carrying markers that no other service on that endpoint emits.

## Notes

- Server-side only; the client ignores it. It round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 — the header matches all existing `.pb.go` files (`check-proto` passes; I verified the unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain first).

## Tests

- `Test_SetResponseHeader`: default / override / removal via empty value.
- `Test_WriteResponseHeader_ResponseHeaders`: CORS default, override, removal, custom header addition, origin echo.
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: fix(macos): restore VPN DNS after network changes
issues.body:
## Problem

The standalone macOS client writes VPN DNS into `Setup:/Network/Service/<UUID>/DNS` at connection time. When macOS refreshes network configuration and removes or replaces that override, the AWG/WireGuard tunnel can remain connected while applications use DHCP DNS. No DNS-change listener reapplies the VPN settings.

This addresses the DNS-loss case reported in [this comment on #3267](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/issues/3267#issuecomment-6070869518). It does not address the separate gateway/ARP failure in the original report.

## Change

- Subscribe to network-service and DNS keys once per DNS utility lifetime, and repair only while the VPN DNS override is active. Deliver native notifications to the Qt object thread through a serial dispatch queue.
- Reapply the desired DNS only when it differs, including for newly added services. Keep the original backup across repairs and repeated updates.
- Disable repair before restoration, invalidate queued work across reconnects, and retain callback context independently of object lifetime. Cancel the native subscription only at destruction: immediate unsubscribe/resubscribe can fail while asynchronous cancellation is still pending.
- Report registration/read/write failures; distinguish missing keys from read errors and preserve failed restoration backups for retry. Do not recreate removed services.
- Add a standalone macOS QtTest suite that compiles the production DNS class, using an in-memory SystemConfiguration boundary without changing host DNS.

## Validation

On Apple silicon, macOS 26.6.2, Xcode 27.1, Qt 6.11.2:

- Original code reproduced deletion recovery, backup corruption, and failure-reporting regressions before the fix.
- Standalone QtTest suite: **21 passed, 0 failed** (19 scenarios plus initialization/cleanup).
- Same suite passed with **AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer**.
- A read-only native SystemConfiguration probe reproduced `kSCStatusNotifierActive` on the second immediate subscribe/unsubscribe cycle. The follow-up regression models pending cancellation and passes with the lifetime subscription.
- Changed production source and MOC compiled against real SystemConfiguration declarations and the production logger, without test API redirects.
- `git diff --check` passed.

issues.title: WG/AWG .conf import silently ignores a single DNS server and uses application DNS
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

Importing a valid WireGuard `.conf` file with exactly one IPv4 DNS server silently discards that DNS setting. On Android, the resulting VPN network receives the application's DNS values instead of the server specified in the file.

The connection itself succeeds, so this is easy to miss when public names still resolve. It breaks resolution of private names available only through the configured resolver.

**Environment**

- AmneziaVPN: 5.0.3.0
- Client OS: Android 16
- Protocol tested: ordinary WireGuard, without AmneziaWG obfuscation
- Profile imported from a `.conf` file

**To Reproduce**

1. Take a working WireGuard configuration and specify a single reachable IPv4 DNS server in `[Interface]`, for example:
   ```ini
   DNS = 10.23.0.53
   ```
   This is an illustrative private address, not an address from the tested setup.
2. Leave the application DNS settings at their defaults (`1.1.1.1` and `1.0.0.1`).
3. Import the file as a new profile and connect.
4. Inspect the active VPN network's `DnsAddresses` in `adb shell dumpsys connectivity`.

**Actual behavior**

The configured private resolver is absent. The captured VPN network state contained:

```text
InterfaceName: tun0
DnsAddresses: [ /1.1.1.1,/1.0.0.1 ]
```

The intended private DNS server was independently tested from the phone: a direct UDP/53 DNS query returned a successful response. This is a DNS configuration/import problem, rather than evidence that the intended resolver is unreachable.

Android Private DNS was in automatic (`opportunistic`) mode during the captured baseline. The incorrect addresses were already present in the VPN's `DnsAddresses`; this report concerns which servers the VPN registers with Android, not a DNS leak-test website's result.

**Expected behavior**

A valid single DNS address in an imported WireGuard configuration should be retained and applied to the VPN network. It should not silently disappear because no second DNS address is provided.

**Source-level cause**

In tag `5.0.3.0`, `ImportController::extractWireGuardConfig()` uses a DNS regular expression with two mandatory IPv4 capture groups. It only populates the profile's `dns1` and `dns2` when that entire expression matches:

https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/5.0.3.0/client/core/controllers/selfhosted/importController.cpp#L645-L652

Consequently:

- `DNS = 10.23.0.53` does not match.
- `DNS = 10.23.0.53, 10.23.0.54` matches.

When profile DNS fields are absent, `NativeServerConfig::getDnsPair()` falls back to the application settings:

https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/5.0.3.0/client/core/models/selfhosted/nativeServerConfig.cpp#L38-L49

The application defaults are `1.1.1.1` and `1.0.0.1`:

https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/5.0.3.0/client/core/repositories/secureAppSettingsRepository.cpp#L74-L88

The same import function handles both WireGuard and AmneziaWG profiles. The device-level reproduction above used ordinary WireGuard.

**Workaround**

Add a second reachable private DNS server to the same line and import the modified file as a new profile:

```ini
DNS = 10.23.0.53, 10.23.0.54
```

After this change, the previously failing name resolution in Chrome started working in the tested setup.

**Suggested fix**

Parse the DNS field as a list and preserve a valid single entry. Add regression coverage for a single IPv4 DNS address and two comma-separated IPv4 addresses, including verification that the single-entry case does not silently fall back to the application primary DNS.

**Related issues**

- #2957 concerns imported profile DNS taking precedence over application settings. This report concerns a valid single DNS entry being lost during import.
- #3059 reports ignored DNS settings on Android, without identifying this single-entry parsing failure.

issues.title: fix(windows): initialize split tunnel driver lazily to stop paged pool leak
issues.body:
Fixes #3216.

## Problem

With app split tunneling unused, kernel paged pool grows without bound while `AmneziaVPN-service` runs and is only freed by a reboot (or a service restart).

`WindowsSplitTunnel::create()` → `initDriver()` sends `IOCTL_INITIALIZE` at daemon start. In `mullvad-split-tunnel.sys`, initialization registers the process-notify routine, which allocates one `PROCESS_EVENT` (tag `SPTU`, paged pool) for every process arrival and departure and appends it to `EventQueue` ([procmon.cpp](https://github.com/mullvad/win-split-tunnel/blob/main/src/procmon/procmon.cpp)). The worker drains the queue only after `procmon::EnableDispatching()`, i.e. after `IOCTL_REGISTER_PROCESSES`.

The daemon sends `IOCTL_REGISTER_PROCESSES` only from `start()`, when the config has excluded apps. Otherwise it calls `stop()` → `IOCTL_CLEAR_CONFIGURATION`, which the driver does not accept in `STATE_INITIALIZED` (only `IOCTL_REGISTER_PROCESSES` is valid there), so the queue never drains.

## Fix

- `initDriver()`: still resets a driver left at `>= STATE_INITIALIZED`, but no longer sends `IOCTL_INITIALIZE`; the driver stays in `STATE_STARTED`, where no process events are queued. `start()` already sends `IOCTL_INITIALIZE` when it finds `STATE_STARTED`, so enabling app split tunneling works as before.
- `stop()`: returns early in `STATE_STARTED`; in `STATE_INITIALIZED` (a `start()` that failed before process registration) it sends `IOCTL_ST_RESET`, which is valid in that state and tears down the process monitor, freeing the queue. `READY` / `RUNNING` keep the existing `IOCTL_CLEAR_CONFIGURATION` path (dispatching is enabled there, so the queue drains).
- Constructor assert and header comment updated to `STATE_STARTED`.

## Measurements (before the fix)

Windows 11, AmneziaVPN 5.0.1.5, `mullvad-split-tunnel.sys` 1.2.5.0, app split tunneling not configured:

- after 12 days of uptime: 31.6 M live `SPTU` allocations, 3.7 GB of paged pool (read with `NtQuerySystemInformation(SystemPoolTagInformation)`);
- about 5.5 records leaked per `cmd.exe /c exit` (cmd + conhost, arrival + departure), measured over 1000 runs with the background rate subtracted.

## Testing

Not built locally (no Qt toolchain on this machine). The change was checked against the driver's IOCTL state machine (`driverentry.cpp`, `ioctl.cpp` `Reset()`), and the leak was measured live on the release build above. Reviewers with a Windows build: with app split tunneling off, `SPTU` live allocations should stay flat while processes start and exit; turning app split tunneling on should still reach `STATE_RUNNING`.

issues.title: [Feature Request] Support for non-systemd Linux distributions (OpenRC, runit, dinit, s6, SysVinit)
issues.body:
I recently encountered a major problem: when I tried running AmneziaVPN on Gentoo Linux with OpenRC, the client immediately failed and crashed. When I reached out to official support, they couldn't help since non-systemd distributions are not officially supported. ( This relates to the problems discussed in #775 and #3000)

So I decided to investigate what was actually causing the failure and built a working solution myself.
After digging into the logs and daemon behavior, I found that `AmneziaVPN-service` itself is a standard Qt process and doesn't actually need systemd. The failures come down to three specific external dependencies:
1. The installer hardcodes `systemctl`, failing on any alternative init system.
2. Strict reliance on `systemd-resolved` via D-Bus (`org.freedesktop.resolve1`): when Amnezia connects, it applies `iptables` drop rules for port 53, but because `systemd-resolved` doesn't exist, the DNS configuration fails completely. The result is a connected tunnel with zero working Internet.
3. Improper lifecycle and socket handling: killing the process leaves stale Unix sockets in `/tmp/`, causing immediate `EADDRINUSE` crash loops on restart, while stopping the daemon leaves orphaned `amnvpn.*` chains cluttering the firewall.

To solve this for Gentoo, Artix, Void, and other non-systemd distros, I created a universal compatibility layer with a lightweight D-Bus DNS bridge and supervised service scripts:
Repo: https://github.com/Werko1a/amneziavpn-non-systemd

It has been thoroughly tested and verified on an Artix Linux VM (OpenRC):
- Service cleanly survives `kill -9` without stale socket deadlocks;
- DNS resolves properly through the tunnel via the D-Bus shim;
- Firewall rules are completely purged across all tables on service stop.

*(The initial scaffolding was assisted by AI tools, but every script, template, and fix has been manually verified, debugged, and tested on an Artix Linux OpenRC environment).*

issues.title: macOS: client from `dev` hangs at startup in libagw (Go runtime `sigaltstack` fails with EPERM)
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**
A macOS client built from `dev` (after #3028 "use libagw") hangs right after launch. The window appears, then the app stops responding and uses one core at 100%. Release 5.0.4.2, which does not include libagw, starts normally when built the same way.

The main thread is stuck in the Go runtime of libagw:

```
main
 → AmneziaApplication::init
 → UpdateController::checkForUpdates
 → GatewayController::GatewayController
 → agw_client_create
 → crosscall2            (first call into Go from the main thread)
 → runtime.sigaltstack_trampoline
 → runtime.notok         (str x8, [x8]; b .)
```

`sigaltstack` returns -1 with `errno = EPERM`, so the runtime calls `notok`, which writes to address 0. The resulting SIGSEGV is caught and the faulting instruction runs again, so the thread spins forever instead of crashing.

On this first cgo callback the runtime finds the main thread's alternate signal stack disabled and tries to install its own (`minitSignalStack` → `signalstack`). The kernel refuses because the thread's signal stack flags already have `SS_ONSTACK` set:

| Point (main thread) | `sigaltstack(NULL, &ss).ss_flags` |
|---|---|
| `main`, start of `AmneziaApplication::init` | `SS_DISABLE` (4) |
| after `QQmlApplicationEngine::load` | `SS_ONSTACK \| SS_DISABLE` (5) |
| `UpdateController::checkForUpdates`, `crosscall2` | `SS_ONSTACK \| SS_DISABLE` (5) |

No `sigaltstack`, `sigaction` or `_sigtramp` runs on the main thread during `QQmlApplicationEngine::load`, so I could not find what sets the flag. `sigaltstack` calls made by Go on its own threads (32 KiB stacks) succeed.

**To Reproduce**
1. Build `dev` for macOS: `deploy/build.sh --generator Ninja --installer all` (Qt 6.10.1, libagw 1.0.8 built with Go 1.27.1 from the Conan remote).
2. Launch `AmneziaVPN.app`.
3. The UI loads, then the app hangs. Under lldb the main thread stops with `EXC_BAD_ACCESS (address=0x0)` in `runtime.notok`.

**Expected behavior**
The app starts, and `GatewayController` creates the libagw client without hanging the main thread.

**Log files**
Nothing relevant is logged before the hang: the last lines are the normal startup messages.

**Desktop:**
 - OS: macOS 26.3.1, Apple Silicon (arm64)
 - Version: `dev` at 3121775a (5.1.0.3), local build

**Additional context**
- Ideas for a workaround, not tested: create the libagw client off the main thread, or install an alternate signal stack on the main thread early in `main()` so the Go runtime adopts it instead of trying to set its own.
- Possibly related on the Go side: golang/go#80622 (darwin/arm64 cgo callbacks from host threads).

issues.title: fix: apply KillSwitch DNS exceptions for AWG/WireGuard on macOS and Linux
issues.body:
## Problem

With KillSwitch enabled and an AmneziaWG/WireGuard connection, DNS servers added to **Settings → KillSwitch → DNS Exceptions** are still blocked on macOS. The same code path is used on Linux.

The exceptions do reach the daemon: `localsocketcontroller.cpp` sends `allowedDnsServers`, and `Daemon::parseConfig` stores them in `InterfaceConfig::m_allowedDnsServers`. But only the Windows firewall (`windowsfirewall.cpp`) and the OpenVPN/Xray path (`service/server/killswitch.cpp`) use that list. On macOS and Linux, `WireguardUtils*::addInterface` builds `FirewallParams::dnsServers` from the primary and secondary DNS only, so the `310.blockDNS` rule keeps blocking the exception servers.

## Change

In `client/platforms/macos/daemon/wireguardutilsmacos.cpp` and `client/platforms/linux/daemon/wireguardutilslinux.cpp`, append `config.m_allowedDnsServers` to `params.dnsServers`, the same way the secondary DNS is added.

The list is joined into a `pfctl`/`iptables` command that runs through `bash -c` as root, and `Daemon::parseStringList` only checks that entries are strings. So each entry is validated with `QHostAddress`: anything that is not a plain IP address, or that has a scope id, is skipped with a warning.

## Testing

On macOS, with an AmneziaWG connection, KillSwitch enabled and DNS servers in DNS Exceptions:

- Before: the exception servers were unreachable on port 53 (UDP and TCP), and the `amn/310.blockDNS` `dnsaddr` table held only the connection's own DNS.
- After: the exception servers answer over UDP and TCP. DNS to servers outside the list is still blocked, while other traffic to those servers passes, so the KillSwitch DNS rule stays in force.

Verified on a 5.0.4.2 build with this patch applied; the changed code is identical in `dev`. The Linux change was not tested on a Linux machine; it relies on CI to build it.

**Workaround** (in case it helps others): add the routes yourself with a NetworkManager dispatcher script, `/etc/NetworkManager/dispatcher.d/90-bypass-vpn` (root, 755):

```sh
#!/bin/sh
IFACE="$1"; ACTION="$2"
NETS="185.73.192.0/22 212.164.138.0/24 212.164.140.0/24 217.175.128.0/19"
[ "$(nmcli -g GENERAL.TYPE device show "$IFACE" 2>/dev/null)" = "wifi" ] || exit 0
case "$ACTION" in
    up|dhcp4-change)
        [ -n "$IP4_GATEWAY" ] || exit 0
        for net in $NETS; do ip route replace "$net" via "$IP4_GATEWAY" dev "$IFACE"; done ;;
esac
```

With it, the traffic for these sites goes through `wlp1s0`, everything else still goes through `amn0`. Note: this does not work with the kill switch enabled — its firewall drops the non-tunnel traffic.

_Edit: an earlier version of this comment said the list was applied "partially". That was wrong: the extra routes were leftovers from the XRay session._

comments.issue_title: feature: enhance site split tunneling
comments.body:
### Feature request: Country-aware split tunneling — route international traffic through VPN, local traffic directly

I'd like to add a concrete use case from mainland China to this feature request.

I use AmneziaVPN while traveling through Asia. The VPN itself performs very well, but split tunneling for Chinese services remains challenging.

For comparison, I've used Astrill's ASUS router applet for years with its **"Tunnel Only International Sites"** setting. This automatically routes domestic Chinese destinations directly through the local ISP while sending international traffic through the VPN.

It works particularly well for services such as Taobao, JD.com, Alibaba, Alipay, and WeChat.

With AmneziaVPN, I'm currently working with an exclusion list containing 118 hostnames. However, manually resolving domains into IP addresses is cumbersome and can be unreliable as CDN addresses and DNS responses change.

**Suggested functionality**

- Provide an optional **"Bypass local country / Tunnel international destinations"** mode, with a manually selectable country (e.g., China).
- Use regularly updated geographic IP routing data to bypass domestic IP ranges while keeping other traffic inside the VPN.
- Allow individual domain/IP overrides for exceptions and incorrectly classified destinations.
- Handle DNS consistently with the selected routing policy, without unexpectedly exposing DNS queries intended to use the VPN.
- Implement updates efficiently so large country-level routing tables don't introduce connection delays or client instability.
- Ideally support this across WireGuard, AmneziaWG, and other protocols.

This could be useful not only in China but also in Iran, Russia, and other countries where users need international VPN access alongside fast and reliable domestic connectivity.

I noticed the discussion in #3123 about GeoIP/GeoSite routing data and the performance challenges of large route lists. Perhaps that work could provide a foundation.

**The desired experience is simple:** connect once, let domestic services use the local ISP, and let international destinations use the VPN, without maintaining extensive exclusion lists manually.

Thank you for developing and maintaining AmneziaVPN. It's already an excellent option for self-hosted VPN access, and this would make it considerably more practical for everyday use in China.

issues.title: feat(tun): add an L3 TUN that carries whole IP packets
issues.body:
## Summary

Adds an optional `l3tun` mode that copies whole IP packets between a local TUN device and QUIC datagrams. It does not terminate TCP or UDP. The intended use is to run VXLAN (or any other IP protocol) between the two TUNs, so the overlay keeps a normal 1500-byte inner MTU instead of squeezing VXLAN through `udpForwarding` and a reduced MTU.

Both ends opt in. The client sends `Hysteria-L3: true` on the existing auth request only when `l3tun` is configured, and the server grants it only when it has `l3tun` as well. The header is also sent as `false` otherwise; an older peer ignores the unknown header. L3 datagrams use session id 0 and a zero address-length byte, which `ParseUDPMessage` already rejects, so an older peer drops them.

## How packets are carried

One IP packet is sent as one QUIC datagram. If that datagram is larger than the peer's current payload limit (`quic.DatagramTooLargeError`), it is split into evenly sized fragments.

The datagram prefix is 11 bytes:

```
SessionID u32 = 0 | PacketID low 16 | FragID u8 | FragCount u8 | 0x00 | PacketID high 16 | IP packet
```

Fragments of different packets may interleave and are reassembled by the 32-bit packet id. A missing fragment drops the whole packet. There is no fragment retransmission; an inner TCP retransmits. Reassembly gives up after 200 ms. The largest IP packet is 1600 bytes. A 1600-byte packet under the usual 1200-byte datagram frame is two fragments of about 800 bytes.

The server keeps one L3 peer: the latest authenticated client that requested L3 replaces the previous one. Packets read from the local TUN while no peer is connected are discarded. Before a received packet is written into the local TUN, its source address must equal the configured `peer`.

The client L3 device stays up across QUIC reconnects. Traffic is counted with the existing `TrafficLogger`, in the same direction as UDP proxying.

`l3tun` is supported on Linux, Darwin, Windows, and Android (sing-tun). Creating the device needs root or `CAP_NET_ADMIN`. Hysteria creates and addresses `hytun0` only. The operator adds the VXLAN interface after the TUN exists. VXLAN's UDP port stays inside the tunnel, so it does not need a public firewall opening.

## Configuration

Client:

```yaml
l3tun:
  name: hytun0
  mtu: 1600
  address: 10.200.0.2/30
  peer: 10.200.0.1
```

Server:

```yaml
l3tun:
  name: hytun0
  mtu: 1600
  address: 10.200.0.1/30
  peer: 10.200.0.2
```

`mtu` defaults to 1600 and cannot be higher. `address` is a prefix; `peer` must be the same IP version. A `/30` gives a connected route, so this tunnel does not need IP forwarding and does not capture the path back to the server's public address.

Operator notes, including the VXLAN commands, are in `VXLAN.md` (currently written in Chinese). For an inner MTU of 1500 the outer packet is about 1550 bytes (Ethernet 14 + VXLAN 8 + UDP 8 + IPv4 20), which fits in the 1600-byte TUN without kernel fragmentation:

```bash
ping -M do -s 1472 -c 3 10.201.0.1
```

## Test results

Measured on this branch, Linux amd64 at both ends. `hytun0` MTU 1600. VXLAN between the two TUN addresses. Path: a residential PPPoE link (uplink about 40 Mbps) to a Tokyo VPS, then to a second Tokyo host running iperf3 3.16. The iperf3 client is 3.9. Brutal limits on the client were 90 Mbps up and 200 Mbps down, with loss compensation disabled. The QUIC max datagram frame size is 1200 bytes.

Same-region control, VPS to the iperf3 host, 8 seconds: 4374 Mbps up, 4441 Mbps down. The iperf3 server is not the bottleneck.

Tunnel RTT to that host, 10/10: min / avg / max 60.4 / 66.3 / 97.9 ms.

Each VXLAN MTU below is one 10-second single TCP stream in each direction. Numbers are receiver goodput. Retransmissions are the sender's 10-second total. "Outer IP" is `vx MTU + 50`. issues.title: fix(scripts): start server units after network-online.target
issues.body:
The systemd units written by `install_server.sh` only order after `network.target`. That target means the network stack is configured, not that the network is up, so on some boots the server starts before DNS works.

The server resolves hostnames while it loads its config. One example is the realm STUN servers. When that lookup fails at boot, the service exits with:

```
FATAL failed to load server config {"error": "invalid config: realm.stun: lookup <stun host>: i/o timeout"}
```

The unit has no `Restart=`, so it stays down until someone starts it by hand.

This change adds `Wants=network-online.target` and `After=network-online.target` to the server unit template, which systemd documents for services that need a working network at startup: https://systemd.io/NETWORK_ONLINE/
